passages.happening:
The LORD speaks of a person who “sins and acts unfaithfully against the LORD by deceiving his neighbor” (verse 2). He may have kept something left in his care, or stolen, or forced money out of someone, or found lost property and lied about it, and then sworn falsely that he had not (verses 2-3).

When he owns his guilt, he must give back what he took. “He must make restitution in full, add a fifth of the value, and pay it to the owner on the day he acknowledges his guilt” (verse 5).

Then he brings a ram to the priest as a guilt offering. “In this way the priest will make atonement for him before the LORD, and he will be forgiven for anything he may have done to incur guilt” (verse 7).
passages.hearers:
In a world without banks, people left money, animals and goods with a neighbor for safekeeping. Disputes followed. Where there was no proof, a case was settled by an oath before the LORD (Exodus 22:11).

This law is about the man who got away with it. He kept what was not his, and he swore he had not. No court has caught him. The only witness against him is his own conscience. The law speaks to that conscience and gives him a way back.

Two things in the passage would have struck a first hearer.

The first is whom the sin is against. He cheated his neighbor, and the text calls it acting ‘unfaithfully against the LORD’. Leviticus will not let the two be pulled apart. A person cannot be right with God while leaving a neighbor unpaid.

The second is the order. Repayment comes first, with a fifth added, ‘on the day he acknowledges his guilt’. Only then does he bring the ram. He cannot go to the altar to get out of going to his neighbor.

This is plainly a deliberate sin, a lie told under oath. Yet the passage ends with the same promise as the others: ‘he will be forgiven’. The way back is open to someone who did wrong knowingly, if he will come forward, confess and repair the harm.
passages.later:
Numbers repeats the law and adds confession by name: he “must confess the sin he has committed. He must make full restitution, add a fifth to its value, and give all this to the one he has wronged” (Numbers 5:7).

Jesus taught the same order: “First go and be reconciled to your brother; then come and offer your gift” (Matthew 5:24).

When the tax collector Zacchaeus met Jesus, he went further than a fifth: “if I have cheated anyone, I will repay it fourfold” (Luke 19:8). Jesus answered, “Today salvation has come to this house” (Luke 19:9).
passages.asks: No one had caught this man; the law spoke to him anyway. Ask whether there is something you got away with that still needs putting right. And ask whether you have ever gone to God for forgiveness to avoid going to the person you wronged.

passages.t: The fire that must not go out
passages.happening:
Now the LORD gives instructions for Aaron and his sons. “The burnt offering is to remain on the hearth of the altar all night, until morning, and the fire must be kept burning on the altar” (verse 9).

In the morning the priest puts on his linen clothes and clears the ashes from the altar. Then he changes into other clothes and carries the ashes outside the camp to a clean place (verses 10-11). He adds wood, lays out the burnt offering, and burns the fat of the peace offerings (verse 12).

“The fire shall be kept burning on the altar continually; it must not be extinguished” (verse 13).
passages.hearers:
At this point the book changes its audience. Chapters 1 to 5 told the ordinary worshiper what to bring. From here to the end of chapter 7 the same offerings are gone through again from the priests' side of the altar. Each section begins the same way: ‘this is the law of’ an offering. The Hebrew word for ‘law’ is torah, which means instruction. These are the working rules for men who will handle holy things every day.

This short paragraph makes one point three times: the fire must be kept burning (verses 9, 12 and 13). The evening offering smoldered on the altar all night. The altar was never cold. At any hour, the sign that Israel belonged to God was still burning.

Notice the humble work. Clearing ashes is a chore, and the priest does it in his sacred linen. Then he changes before he carries the ashes out of the camp. Even the dirty jobs of God's house are done with care, and the holy and the ordinary are kept apart.
passages.later:
On the day the priests began their work, fire came from God onto this altar: “Fire came out from the presence of the LORD and consumed the burnt offering” (Leviticus 9:24).

The letter to the Hebrews speaks of a priestly service that never stops: Christ “is able to save completely those who draw near to God through Him, since He always lives to intercede for them” (Hebrews 7:25). The fire of this chapter has sometimes been read as a picture with a meaning in every detail. The New Testament does not read it that way, and the link here is one of theme only.
passages.asks: Someone had to get up every morning, clear the ashes and add wood. Ask what small, daily, unseen task keeps your life with God alive. And ask who does the humble work in your church or home that no one notices, and whether you have thanked them.

passages.t: The grain offering, and the priests' own
passages.happening:
“Now this is the law of the grain offering” (verse 14). The priest burns a handful with the frankincense as the memorial portion. “Aaron and his sons are to eat the remainder. It must be eaten without leaven in a holy place; they are to eat it in the courtyard of the Tent of Meeting” (verse 16). It is “most holy, like the sin offering and the guilt offering” (verse 17).

Then a separate rule. From the day he is anointed, the high priest offers his own grain offering, a tenth of an ephah of fine flour, “half of it in the morning and half in the evening” (verse 20). It is made with oil on a griddle. “Every grain offering for a priest shall be burned completely; it is not to be eaten” (verse 23).
passages.hearers:
Chapter 2 said that the rest of the grain offering belonged to the priests. Here the priests are told how to eat it: without leaven, in the courtyard of the tent, and only by the men of Aaron's family. God calls it ‘their portion of My offerings’ (verse 17). The priests owned no farmland. They ate from God's table.

The priests' own grain offering is different. It is burned whole. A priest cannot give a gift to God and then eat it himself. When the priest is the giver, all of it goes to God.

And the high priest brings this small offering every day, morning and evening. The man at the top of Israel's worship is himself a worshiper who must come with a gift like everyone else.

Verse 18 says, “Anything that touches them will become holy.” In Leviticus, holiness is more than a moral quality. It is a state: the condition of belonging to God. The book speaks of it almost as a force that passes by touch. Readers differ on the details. Some take the words as a plain statement that contact passes holiness on. Others read them as a warning that whoever touches these things must be holy, so that only the priests may handle them. Many think the rule applied mainly to objects.
passages.later:
The prophet Haggai once put the question to the priests of his day. Does holy meat carried in a garment make other food holy? “‘No,’ replied the priests” (Haggai 2:12). But they agreed that the uncleanness of a dead body did pass on (Haggai 2:13).

Ezekiel, picturing a new temple, has the priests change their clothes before going out to the people, “so that they do not transmit holiness to the people with their garments” (Ezekiel 44:19).

Paul points to the priests' food when he writes about the support of those who preach: “those who work in the temple eat of its food” (1 Corinthians 9:13).
passages.asks: The high priest, of all people, had to bring his own offering twice a day. Ask whether those who lead worship where you are also have room to be worshipers. And if you serve others in God's name, ask when you last came to him with nothing to do for anyone else.

passages.happening:
The priests are told, “this is the law of the sin offering: In the place where the burnt offering is slaughtered, the sin offering shall be slaughtered before the LORD; it is most holy” (verse 25).

“The priest who offers it shall eat it; it must be eaten in a holy place, in the courtyard of the Tent of Meeting” (verse 26). If its blood spatters a garment, the garment is washed in a holy place. A clay pot in which it was boiled must be broken, and a bronze pot scoured and rinsed (verses 27-28).

“But no sin offering may be eaten if its blood has been brought into the Tent of Meeting to make atonement in the Holy Place; it must be burned” (verse 30).
passages.hearers:
It may surprise a reader that the offering for sin is called ‘most holy’. One might expect it to be treated as something tainted. It is the opposite. What God gives to deal with sin is among the holiest things in Israel.

So it is handled with great care. The priest who offers it eats it, in the courtyard and nowhere else. A splash of its blood on a robe is washed out in the holy place. Clay is porous and soaks up what is cooked in it, so a clay pot is broken; a bronze pot can be scrubbed clean.

The last verse makes an exception. Chapter 4 said that when the high priest or the whole people sinned, the blood was carried inside the tent. No one eats those offerings. They are burned outside the camp. The priest does not eat an offering made for his own sin.
passages.later:
In the next story of the book, Moses is angry because a sin offering that should have been eaten was burned instead. He says it was given to the priests “to take away the guilt of the congregation by making atonement for them before the LORD” (Leviticus 10:17).

The letter to the Hebrews draws on verse 30: “the high priest brings the blood of animals into the Holy Place as a sacrifice for sin”, and “the bodies are burned outside the camp” (Hebrews 13:11). It goes on to say that Jesus “suffered outside the city gate” (Hebrews 13:12).
passages.asks: The offering for sin was called most holy. Ask whether you treat God's forgiveness as a holy thing, or as something common that can be taken for granted. And ask what care you take with the things, and the people, that belong to God.
